title: Victim loses £250k after scammers use AI video of 'well-known' celebrity

reading.body:
This is a synthetic media fraud, in which an AI-generated video impersonated a well-known financial figure to lend credibility to an investment that did not exist. The impersonation sat at the top of the funnel, in the advertisement itself, and everything after it, the WhatsApp contact, the account openings, the remote access, the pressure to borrow, was conventional fraud running on the trust the fake video had already bought. The AI did not take the money or make the decisions; it solved the one problem the scammers could not otherwise solve, which is getting a stranger to believe a famous person was recommending them.

The failure is not a model asserting something false in the course of doing its job. It is a generated likeness deployed deliberately, outside any legitimate use, to make a false endorsement look real. Nothing in the deployment chain was built to catch it: the video was made to be seen by people who had no way to check whether the person in it had ever said those words, and the platforms that carried the ad had no check that surfaced to the victim. Catching this would have required verification at the point of the advertisement, not at the point of the bank transfer, by which time the victim was already inside a relationship the scammers controlled.

What is not established is who made the video, which figure it depicted, and whether anyone will be charged. The police described a sophisticated and substantial fraud, which is a finding about the scheme, not a finding about any identified person's intent.

reports.title: Victim loses £250k after scammers use AI video of 'well-known' celebrity

summary:
A person in the Ards and north Down area lost £250,000 after seeing an AI-generated video that appeared to feature a well-known financial figure. The fake advertisement promoted an investment with promised returns. After a small initial payment, the scammers contacted the victim on WhatsApp and pushed for more money. They persuaded the victim to open several online accounts and gave them remote access to their computer, then encouraged borrowing to keep investing. The Police Service of Northern Ireland called it a sophisticated and substantial fraud.

Police did not name the celebrity used in the video, though BBC News NI has seen similar scams using financial experts. The PSNI warned that an apparent celebrity endorsement is not proof an investment is real, and said fraudsters can make convincing ads, websites and messages, including fake videos and voices. Superintendent Joanne Gibson of the Scamwise Partnership urged people to stop and check financial activity and to talk with relatives about fraud. Police advised verifying who you deal with and checking Financial Conduct Authority authorisation.
title_en: Victim loses £250k after scammers use AI video of 'well-known' celebrity
